newsitem.title: UK: IRA kills two Northern Ireland policemen in ambush.
newsitem.headline: IRA kills two Northern Ireland policemen in ambush.

text.p: Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas shot dead two Northern Ireland policemen in an ambush on Monday, heightening fears the British-ruled province faced a return to widespread sectarian violence.
The British government called off further talks with Sinn Fein, the outlawed IRA's political wing, and Protestant leaders appealed for hardliners in their community to "draw back from the brink".

The officers were on routine foot patrol near the centre of the busy town of Lurgan southwest of Belfast when gunmen shot them at close range. A doctor ran from a nearby surgery to help but the men were already dead.
Both men were married with young children.
A caller using an IRA code word rang a Belfast radio station and said the organisation's "North Armagh Brigade" had "carried out this morning's attack".
A spokesman for British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is attending a summit in Amsterdam, said he had been informed about the killing. "He is appalled by this wicked and evil act," he said.
British Northern Ireland minister, Mo Mowlam, speaking before the IRA's admission, described the double murder as an outrage.
"At a time when Northern Ireland is holding its breath and hope for peace, those intent on evil have struck," Mowlam said in statement.
"The government resolutely condemns this atrocity but we will not be intimidated into weakening our resolution to bring about a peaceful Northern Ireland in which all can share."

After the IRA's statement, a spokesman for the Northern Ireland office said there was "no question" of agreeing to meet Sinn Fein, which is barred from multi-party talks on the province's future until the IRA reinstates a ceasefire.
Since Labour won power in a British election on May 1, government officials have held two meetings with Sinn Fein to clarify conditions under which they could be admitted to the talks.
Mowlam had agreed to a third meeting but stressed it would be the last unless the IRA ceasefire, broken by a huge bomb in London in February 1996, was renewed.

Mainstream Irish nationalist and Protestant unionist parties said that the ambush was intended to increase divisions during an annually volatile period of street parades by pro-British Protestant groups.
They appealed to pro-British Loyalist guerrillas, who have operated a shaky truce since October 1994, not to strike back and worsen the province's difficulties.
Mowlam added that it was "vital that nobody takes the law into their own hands and that there is no retaliation in any shape or form".
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, said the murder was bound to inflame tensions and appealed for calm.
"I would ask Loyalists not to play the IRA's game. Now is the time to draw back from the brink."
The IRA seriously wounded a policewoman in a sniper attack in Londonderry in April. Last week IRA members fired on a British army vehicle in the city but no one was hurt.
Loyalists have killed two people in the past year and set off sporadic bombs aimed at republicans, apparently in retaliation for republican hostilities.
